'''David Henry Solomon''' {{post-nominals|country=AUS|AC}} (born 19 November 1929) is an Australian [[polymer chemistry|polymer chemist]]. He is best known for his work in developing [[Living free-radical polymerization|Living Radical Polymerization]] techniques, and [[polymer banknote]]s.

==Education==
David Henry Solomon was born 19 November 1929 in [[Adelaide, South Australia]].<ref name=CSIRO>{{cite web |title= David Henry (Dave) Solomon |url= https://csiropedia.csiro.au/solomon-david-henry/ |website= CSIROpedia |date= 13 January 2015 |accessdate= 10 June 2016 }}</ref> He received an Associate of [[Sydney Technical College]], (equivalent to a Diploma of Chemistry) in 1950 and went on to complete a Bachelor of Science (BSc (Hons)) in 1952 from the New South Wales University of Technology (now the [[University of New South Wales]]), a Master of Science (MSc) from the same university in 1955, and a PhD from the University of New South Wales in 1959 with a thesis entitled ''Studies on the Chemistry of Carbonyl Compounds''. In 1968 he was awarded a DSc from the University of New South Wales for his thesis ''Studies on the Chemistry of Coating Compounds''.<ref name="profile">[http://www.chemeng.unimelb.edu.au/people/staff.php?person_ID=13900 University of Melbourne profile page] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701101439/http://www.chemeng.unimelb.edu.au/people/staff.php?person_ID=13900 |date=1 July 2016 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref> He also received an [[Honorary degree|Honorary Doctorate]] in Applied Science from the [[University of Melbourne]] in 2005,<ref>[http://about.unimelb.edu.au/tradition-of-excellence/notable-staff-and-alumni/honorary-degrees University of Melbourne Honorary Degrees] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160704033159/http://about.unimelb.edu.au/tradition-of-excellence/notable-staff-and-alumni/honorary-degrees |date=4 July 2016 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref> one of only seven awarded in the university's history.

==Career==
Solomon joined British Australian Lead Manufacturers Pty Ltd (BALM, which later became [[Dulux|Dulux Australia Ltd]]) as a trainee chemist in 1946 at the age of 16. It was here that he developed his lifelong interest in polymers, and made important observations that the current theories on polymers did not match with what was actually happening in the industrial processes.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

Solomon's strong interest in polymer research drew him to join [[Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation|CSIRO]] as a senior research scientist in the Division of Applied Mineralogy in 1963. In 1970 Solomon transferred to the Division of Applied Chemistry where he established the Polymer Research Group, before going on to become chief of the Division of Applied Organic Chemistry during a reorganisation in 1974, a position he held for the next 17 years.<ref name=CSIRO />

In 1990 he accepted an invitation to become the ICI Australia – Masson Professor and head of the School of Chemistry at the University of Melbourne. Here he started the Polymer Science Group,<ref name="psg">[http://www.chemeng.unimelb.edu.au/polymer-science/ Polymer Science Group website] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160701095836/http://www.chemeng.unimelb.edu.au/polymer-science/ |date=1 July 2016 }}</ref> his third internationally acclaimed polymer research group. After ‘retirement’ in 1995 David took up the position of honorary professorial fellow in the Department of Chemical and Biomolecular Engineering at the university, moving the Polymer Science Group, to which he still acts as senior advisor.<ref name="psg" /> In 2015 he was awarded the title of professor [[emeritus]] at the University of Melbourne.{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

Solomon is often referred to as the father of polymer research in Australia, having established three internationally acclaimed polymer research groups in industry (Dulux, 1960), in Australia's peak scientific research organisation, CSIRO (1970) and at the University of Melbourne (1990).{{citation needed|date=October 2025}}

==Research achievements==
Solomon is well known for several of his research achievements. In particular his work on free radical polymerization revolutionized the field through the development of the first [[living free-radical polymerization]] technique; [[Nitroxide mediated radical polymerization|Nitroxide Mediated Polymerization]] (NMP). He also led the team, and was principal inventor of the world's first [[polymer banknote]].

===Free Radical Polymerization===
Solomon's ground-breaking work on free radical polymerization was initiated through observations made in industry. For example, anomalies that were not explained by polymerization theory at the time, and the observation that during the production of polymer/mineral composites some batches underwent spontaneous combustion. This led to discoveries that had significant influence on the future directions of radical chemistry. It led to the development of Nitroxide Mediated Polymerization (NMP), the first example of a controlled, or living, radical polymerization technique. This research also produced early examples of what was to become known as RAFT, or [[Reversible addition−fragmentation chain-transfer polymerization]]. Solomon's work rewrote the theory on [[Radical polymerization|free radical polymerization]], and he was co-author with [[Graeme Moad]] on the definitive reference book: The Chemistry of Radical Polymerization (Moad & Solomon, 2006). Previous theories attempted to explain [[radical polymerization]] on the basis of thermodynamic stability controlling structure. Solomon's work showed that kinetics was the major factor in controlling the way polymer chains formed.

===Polymer banknotes===
Following a major forgery of Australia's [[Banknotes of the Australian dollar|newly introduced $10 notes]] in 1967, Solomon was invited to a meeting about how to make more secure bank notes. Given his background in polymer science Solomon's idea was to print the notes on a [[plastic]] substrate rather than the traditional paper, and incorporate [[Optical variable device|optically variable devices]] – defined as a device that changes its appearance when something external is done to the note.<ref>[http://theconversation.com/proceeds-of-crime-how-polymer-banknotes-were-invented-34642 Proceeds of crime: how plastic banknotes were invented]. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref>

Solomon went on to lead the research team and was the principal inventor of the world's first polymer banknote, with the first note issued into circulation in 1988: the Australian bicentennial $10.<ref>[http://museum.rba.gov.au/displays/polymer-banknotes/ Reserve Bank of Australia Museum]. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref> He has chronicled the history of the development of polymer banknotes in ''The Plastic Banknote: From Concept to Reality'', co-authored with Tom Spurling (published in 2014).<ref name="banknote book">''The Plastic Banknote: From Concept to Reality'', David Solomon & Tom Spurling, CSIRO Publishing, 2014, {{ISBN|9780643094277}}</ref>

==Selected honours==
Solomon has been the recipient of numerous prestigious awards throughout his career. A selected list is outlined below. 
* 2016 [[List of Companions of the Order of Australia|Companion of the Order of Australia]].<ref>[http://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/companion_order_australia.cfm Companion of the Order of Australia recipients] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090911220755/http://itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/companion_order_australia.cfm |date=11 September 2009 }}. Retrieved 13 June 2016.</ref>
* 2011 [[Prime Minister's Prizes for Science|Prime Minister's Prize for Science]], awarded jointly with Dr Ezio Rizzardo.<ref>[http://www.science.gov.au/community/PrimeMinistersPrizesforScience/Recipients/2011/Pages/default.aspx Prime Minister's Prize for Science 2011]</ref>
* 2006 Victoria Prize.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.veski.org.au/previous-victoria-prize-recipients |title=Victoria Prize 2006 |access-date=10 June 2016 |archive-date=15 March 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160315054053/http://www.veski.org.au/previous-victoria-prize-recipients |url-status=dead }}</ref>
* 2001 [[Centenary Medal]].<ref>[https://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/centenary_medal.cfm#recipients Centenary Medal recipients] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140717181605/http://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/centenary_medal.cfm#recipients |date=17 July 2014 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref>
* 1994 [[Clunies-Ross Award|Clunies Ross National Science and Technology Award]].<ref>[http://www.atse.org.au/atse/about/clunies-ross-award/content/about/previous-recipients.aspx Clunies Ross Award past recipients]. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref>
* 1990 [[Order of Australia|Member of the Order of Australia]].<ref>[https://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/member_order_australia.cfm Member of the Order of Australia recipients] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160312230144/https://www.itsanhonour.gov.au/honours/awards/medals/member_order_australia.cfm |date=12 March 2016 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref>
* 1989 [[Australian Academy of Science|Ian William Wark Medal and Lecture]].<ref>[https://www.science.org.au/opportunities-scientists/recognition/honorific-awards/career-awards/ian-wark-medal-and-lecture Ian Wark Medal and Lecture]. Retrieved 10 June 2016.</ref>

==Professional societies==
Solomon's considerable contributions to science have been recognised by his peers through election to the following Academies:
* Fellow of the [[Institution of Chemical Engineers]] (FIChemE, 2007)
* Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] ([[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]], 2004).<ref>[https://royalsociety.org/people/david-solomon-12316/ Royal Society Fellows]. Retrieved on 10 June 2016.</ref>
* Foundation Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering]] ([[List of Fellows of the Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering|FTSE]], 1976).<ref>[https://www.atse.org.au/atse/content/fellows-public/directory.aspx Australian Academy of Technological Sciences and Engineering Fellows] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170408082107/https://www.atse.org.au/atse/content/fellows-public/directory.aspx |date=8 April 2017 }}. Retrieved on 10 June 2016.</ref>
* Fellow of the [[Australian Academy of Science]] ([[List of Fellows of the Australian Academy of Science|FAA]], 1975).<ref>[https://www.science.org.au/fellowship/fellows/professor-david-solomon Australian Academy of Science Fellows]. Retrieved on 10 June 2016.</ref>
* Fellow of the [[Royal Australian Chemical Institute]] (FRACI, 1966)
Solomon has always been active in these societies, in particular the Royal Australian Chemical Institute (RACI). In 2001 the RACI established the Solomon Lecture Series in recognition of his contribution to the field and to the RACI.<ref>[http://www.polymer.org.au/index.php/home/activities/solomon-lectures Solomon Lecture Series] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160624073033/http://www.polymer.org.au/index.php/home/activities/solomon-lectures |date=24 June 2016 }}. Retrieved 10 June 2016</ref> A biennial series presented by an invited leading international polymer researcher, this Lecture Series recognizes the importance of promoting the exchange of ideas and expertise and to expose young scientists to the best in their field internationally.

==Publications==
Solomon is co-author of nine books, including an historical account of the development of plastic banknotes (''The Plastic Banknote: From Concept to Reality'')<ref name="banknote book" /> and several text books (including ''The Chemistry of Radical Polymerization'').<ref>{{cite book |title=The Chemistry of Radical Polymerization |edition=Second |first1=G. |last1=Moad |first2=D.H. |last2=Solomon |publisher=[[Elsevier]] |year=2006}}</ref> He is also co-author of over 250 journal papers and 45 patents.<ref name="profile" />
